title: Your door among the schools
hookLine: where you feel at home, and why that doesn't make others wrong

cards: A householder named Dasama, from the town of Atthakanagara, goes out of his way to find Ananda, the Buddha's old attendant. He asks a simple question: is there one teaching that opens the way to freedom?

Ananda gives him eleven, one after another: ways of meditating, ways of loving, ways of letting the mind grow wide and still. Dasama is delighted. He was looking for one door, and he has been shown a house full of them.

teach.b: Here is what Dasama says, in the Pali discourse that bears his town's name. Suppose a man's house has eleven doors, and the house catches fire. He could get out safely through any one of them.
In the same way, he says, I can find my way out through any one of these eleven doors. Notice what he doesn't say. He doesn't call the other ten fake, or tear them down once he's out.
He just needs one to walk through. Careful, though: the text is about kinds of meditation, not about schools. But the picture travels well.
Second, the home. Over this block you've met Theravada and Mahayana, the arahant and the bodhisattva, chanting and silence, sudden and gradual, three canons and four languages.
Some of it may have felt like home: a robe color, a style of sitting, a text that spoke to you. Or none of it yet, which is also fine.

teach.h: A DOOR IS NOT A WALL.
teach.b: Third, the wall. A home has a door you use. A wall is built to keep others out.
Choosing where you feel at home doesn't require deciding everyone else is in the wrong house. Dasama's eleven doors all lead out of the same fire.

Fourth, the Kalamas again: you can test a door by what it does for you, and still honor the doors that work for others. Some teachers tell students to go deep in one practice rather than tasting all of them forever.
Walking through it with respect for the other ten is the difference between a home and a wall.

how: A Buddhist may practice within one school or lineage, with its own teachers, texts and customs, while visiting, learning from and celebrating with other schools.

games.q: what does “your door among the schools” mean?
o: the temple entrance that only members may walk through
the school or practice that feels like home to you
the one school a teacher assigns you on the first day

games.q: your door among the schools: tap the pairs.
p: your door, with the others left open

s: Dasama decides the other ten doors are fake once he finds one
he says he can get out by any one of them; he tears none down.
the eleven doors in the text are kinds of meditation, not schools
the discourse is about meditation; the picture of a house with many doors travels further.
finding a home school means deciding the others are wrong
a home has a door you use; a wall keeps others out. choosing one needs no wall.

games.q: you're Dasama. you asked for one teaching, and Ananda has shown you eleven. what do you say?
o: which one is the real one?
like a burning house with eleven doors, I can get out by any one.
eleven is too many; I'll keep looking.
games.why: he's delighted. any one door leads out of the fire, and he needs only one to walk through.

practice: Look back over the schools and practices of these weeks and ask, without pushing: where did something in me relax? A chant, a silence, a story, a robe, a teacher's line.
Let one come forward, or let it be that none has yet, and if one does, give it a single quiet sentence that begins: I feel at home in.

wordCard.voice: Your door among the schools. The school or practice that feels like home, chosen without walling anyone else out. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit dvara: a door or gate.

carryVoice: Your line: a home, not a wall. The week closes: three canons, four languages, robes and colors, festivals, meeting each other, no ranking, and your door. I'll be here tomorrow.
